note: CONFLICT: the row's method string is "Symmetric FFN, Relu, 32 features per translation" (and until 2024-07-30 its reference was a parameter file "data/NQS/chain32P_32_1.mpack", varbench/varbench 6e9f6b83), while the script it now links runs nk.models.GCNN with layers = 2, features = 32 and NetKet's default activation reim_selu, not ReLU. The script's network would have 32*1*32 + 32 (DenseSymmFFT) + 32*32*64 + 32 (one DenseEquivariantFFT over the 64-element space group of the 32-site ring: 32 translations x {identity, reflection}) = 66624 real parameters; a one-layer symmetric ReLU FFN as the method string describes would not. parameters is therefore left null and the script's count is only recorded here. samples and iterations are the script's (defaults, unchanged across the program's history) and carry the same doubt. samples = 1024 per optimisation step (MCState n_samples = batch_size; MetropolisLocal with n_chains = batch_size = 1024, one sample per chain per step, each separated by sweep_size = N = 32 proposals (NetKet default), n_discard_per_chain = 0); iterations = 10000 ("--max_step" default=10**4); optimizer SR (VMC_SRt when n_parameters >= n_samples), lr 1e-3. The final energy is then estimated once with estim_size = 1024^2 = 1048576 samples (not an optimisation step). NetKet pinned twice by the program: programs/vmc_netket/requirements.txt "NetKet==3.13.0" and conda_env.yaml "netket=3.11.4"; every NetKet line cited here reads the same at both tags. The energy is older than the script: VarBench's data file listed it with no code link ("TODO: own code", varbench/varbench 0ef1497c and 6e9f6b83, 2024-07-11) until the scripts were added on 2024-07-30 (5047bfd6 RBM, d54f7c01 RNN, 765c5d13 GCNN), which changed only the reference column, so the script documents the settings after the fact, with library versions that may postdate the run. || pass 2026-09-27: evaluation of the linked script only (the row's method string, "Symmetric FFN", is not this network and parameters stay null). The script's GCNN has 66,624 parameters (route1a note) >= n_samples 1024, so nkx.driver.VMC_SRt: sr minsr. proposals_per_sample = N x (1 + 0)/1 = 32 (1024 chains, one sample each, no discard, sweep_size = N). complex left absent: the GCNN's real float32 kernels with NetKet's complex output are not settled here. If the count is ever accepted, reuse is the 64-element space group (verify/agent-A.md), not 32.

note: parameters = Nsite^2 + alpha + 2 + 2 alpha Nsite = 256^2 + 2 + 2 + 2*2*256 = 66564 COMPLEX parameters (ComplexType 1 in every def file; 133128 real numbers): pair-product orbitals f_ij without sublattice structure (NOrbitalIdx = Nsite^2), RBM hidden biases (alpha), physical-layer biases (2, one per spin), and translation-invariant RBM weights (2 alpha Nsite, the 1x1 RBM sublattice sub_rbm_phidx.py generates, as the method string states). samples = NVMCSample x MPI processes / NSplitSize = 100 x 8 / 1 = 800 per SR step: with NSplitSize = 1 every rank is its own sampling group (vmcmain.c "group1 = rank0/NSplitSize"), draws NVMCSample samples after NVMCWarmUp = 100 (each separated by NVMCInterval x Nsite = 256 proposals) and WeightAverageWE sums the weights over all ranks (average.c); iterations = NSROptItrStep = 1000 SR steps (the parameters are averaged over the last NSROptItrSmp = 100). All of these are the defaults of make_modpara, not overridden by the optimisation call. Each amplitude sums a Pfaffian of the 214-electron pair-product state over NSPGaussLeg x |NMPTrans| = 8 x 256 = 2048 spin/momentum projection points. The script's input names the couplings "t1 1.0 ... V1 1.0 V2 0.5", but make_all.py reads loaded_dict.get("V", 0) (and "t2", "V2"), so V = 0 and no coulombinter.def is written: as committed the script does not build this instance's Hamiltonian (the wave function and sampling settings are unaffected). Doubt (why confidence is low): the script is the simplified template of programs/mVMC_makedef/README.txt ("For simplicity, we focus on the case of Ns=8x8"). It runs ONE optimisation stage with the projections and the RBM on from the start, while the README's protocol has three optimisation stages (f_ij alone from the UHF solution, then the RBM, then the projections) whose step counts are not stated anywhere, and it never runs the Lanczos step the energy includes: make_all.py also writes namelist_aft.def/modpara_aft.def (NVMCCalMode=1, NLanczosMode=1, NVMCWarmUp=500, NVMCInterval=5, NVMCSample=5000, NDataQtySmp=10) but mVMC.sh does not call it. So the counts are the script's single stage, not the published run's total. No time is recorded anywhere; "mpiexec -np 8" names MPI processes, not hardware. || pass 2026-09-27: vmc_schedule read from the def files the script generates: n_proc 8 (mpiexec -np 8); NVMCSample 100, NVMCWarmUp 100, NVMCInterval 1, NSplitSize 1, NSROptItrStep 1000 (make_modpara defaults, not overridden by the optimisation call); NSPGaussLeg 8; NExUpdatePath 0 (hops); NQPOptTrans 1 and NSRCG 0 are mVMC defaults (no qpopttrans.def in namelist.def, no NSRCG line in modpara.def). NMPTrans = 256: modpara.def writes APsgn x Nsite = -256 (APFlag 1); readdef.c flips the sign and sets the antiperiodic flag, so the projection sums |NMPTrans| = 256 translations; N_QP = NSPGaussLeg x NMPTrans = 2048 projection terms. n_size = 2 Ne = Ncond = 214 (NlocalSpin 0 for Hubbard). complex true: every def file has ComplexType 1. parameters_real = 2 x 66564 = 133128 (N^2 + alpha + 2 + 2 alpha N complex parameters = 256^2 + 2 + 2 + 1024). make_all.py reads "V", not "V1", so hasInter is False and coulombinter.def is not written: the wave function and sampling are as stated, the Hamiltonian lacks V1/V2 (route1a note). As before: one optimisation stage only (the README's three-stage protocol and the Lanczos step, namelist_aft.def with NVMCSample 5000, are not run by mVMC.sh), so confidence stays low.

The script's own architecture would have 66051 complex parameters (formula below), recorded here only. samples = NVMCSample x MPI processes / NSplitSize = 100 x 8 / 1 = 800 per SR step: with NSplitSize = 1 every rank is its own sampling group (vmcmain.c "group1 = rank0/NSplitSize"), draws NVMCSample samples after NVMCWarmUp = 100 (each separated by NVMCInterval x Nsite = 256 proposals) and WeightAverageWE sums the weights over all ranks (average.c); iterations = NSROptItrStep = 1000 SR steps (the parameters are averaged over the last NSROptItrSmp = 100). reported_as: Appendix C: We note that the training of our ansatz was performed using P100 GPUs. In order to produce the results of Fig. 3(b), we use d_h = 300 and N_s = 100 samples for training. We have first performed annealing on the system size 6 x 6 with N_warmup = 1000, N_annealing = 10000, and an initial pseudo-temperature T_0 = 0.25, while using a fixed learning rate eta = 5 x 10^-4. During each annealing step, we perform N_train = 5 gradient descent steps. In this initial phase, we only apply the U(1) symmetry. In the next phase, we perform an additional 25000 gradients steps at zero pseudo-temperature and add an additional 25000 gradients steps after applying C2d symmetry. [...] We then increase the system size to 8 x 8, while keeping our ansatz parameters fixed, applying C2d symmetry and while using zero pseudo-temperature. In this phase, the learning rate is fixed to eta = 10^-5. After this step, we train our RNN ansatz until convergence. We repeat the same procedure for system sizes 10 x 10, 12 x 12, 14 x 14 and 16 x 16. We note that for 8 x 8, we add 40000 gradient steps. For 10 x 10, we continue training with 20000 gradient steps. For 12 x 12, we converge using 10000 training steps. For 14 x 14, we continue training with 5000 gradient steps. reported_as: Unless otherwise specified, the total number of markov chains is fixed at N_s = 1024 and the learning rate is fixed at 3e-4. We first train the single particle orbitals without backflow for 10^5 VMC iterations. We then multiply all single particle orbitals by a factor of 10^3, set them to the bias of the last layer of the MLP, and randomly initialize the weights to form the initial MLP-NNBF ansatz. The training for the data in Fig. A1 took 3 x 10^6 VMC iterations, followed by 5 x 10^5 VMC iterations with an exponential decay learning rate schedule tuning the learning rate to 1e-7. [...] All optimizations reported in this paper were performed using H100 GPUs on GH200 superchips. [...] the highest energy wavefunction we study, n_h = 128 with energy per site of -0.75066(2) || Sec. II.A: u(n) is the output, an N\times L matrix, of an MLP with input n [...] Here both spin sectors are combined into a single matrix (e.g. N is the sum of the spin up and down electrons and L is twice the number of physical sites) [...] Our MLP is fully connected with two hidden layers each followed by a layer normalization and relu activation. The input layer is set by |n> = |n_0, n_1, ..., n_L> where n_i \in {-1,1} denotes an empty or occupied spin orbital. The last output layer contains a bias but no non-linear function; this bias can be interpreted as a fixed mean-field solution onto which the neural network provides additive configuration-dependent backflow corrections. || Sec. III: A fixed depth multi-layer MLP-NNBF scales as O(n_o n_h + n_h^2 + \alpha n_h n_o^2 + (\alpha n_o)^3) per step where n_o is the number of orbitals and \alpha is the filling fraction. For our system, n_o = L = 128 and \alpha = 0.4375. [...] this crossover happens at n_h = 7168 || Sec. III (PNNBF): U(n) and J(n) are both L\times L matrices output by the MLP (e.g. the last layer of the network has 2L^2 nodes) || App. B: We then multiply all single particle orbitals by a factor of 10^3, set them to the bias of the last layer of the MLP, and randomly initialize the weights to form the initial MLP-NNBF ansatz. || Fig. A2 caption: Each VMC sweep reports the average energy from 100 VMC steps of each of the 1024 VMC chains. || Acknowledgements: The NQS simulations are implemented using internally developed code with JAX [43], Flax [44], and Optax [45]. || arXiv:2510.26906 Eq. reported_as: TABLE I. Benchmark variational energies for the Shastry-Sutherland and J1-J2 models, using deep translationally-symmetry NQS. The corresponding number of parameters, Np, are indicated. J1-J2 (J1 = 1, J2 = 0.5): ConvNext -0.497583(6), Np = 2.6 x 10^5; fViT [16] -0.497634(1), 2.7 x 10^5; ResNet [15] -0.4976921(4), 1.07 x 10^6. || Bringing all of the previous results together, we choose a network of (6,3,3)[2,2] to compute energies for the L = 10 Shastry-Sutherland model and the L = 10 J1-J2 model. || Our optimization protocol makes use of different symmetry stages [16] as shown in fig. 5 (...) We begin the optimization with the bare network, which internally is made to be translationally invariant. We then introduce point group and spin-parity externally (...) First, we symmetrize over the rotational elements of the point group, that is C4 rotations. We then symmetrize over the full point group, adding reflection in the line x = y to the group to be symmetrized over. Finally we add spin parity symmetry (...) Each iteration, we use the SPRING algorithm described in section A to update the parameters. (...) In the numerical experiments for designing the network we typically perform 2500 iterations in each symmetry stage, with a cosine decaying learning rate [82] from 10^-2 to 5 x 10^-3 and a cosine decaying diagonal shift from 10^-2 to 10^-6 in each stage. We use a total of 4092 samples per iteration, with 512 MC chains on each of 8 A100 GPUs (1 sample per chain), each chain performing a single MC sweep of N_MC steps. At the end of the optimization, we freeze the learning rate and diagonal shift, performing 50 additional optimization steps with more samples per chain, discarding half for thermalization. We use 32 chains per GPU and 8196 total samples. This result is already more accurate than that of HFPS [23] while requiring only one-fifteenth of the cost. By directly optimizing the projected, symmetrized state reach a new state-of-the-art energy of −0.76623(1). This surpasses the previous best result −0.766073(6) from NNBF [25] with only one-sixth of the computational cost. reported_as: The Vision Transformer architecture used in this work comprises h = 12 attention heads, n_l = 8 layers, and an embedding dimension of d = 72, resulting in approximately P ~ 4.5 x 10^5 trainable parameters for different system sizes, from L = 18 to L = 42. The input spin configuration sigma is divided into n non-overlapping patches of size b x b [13], each embedded into R^d through a learnable linear transformation (...) In particular, we set b = 3 for the triangular lattice, which is compatible with the Neel 120 degree antiferromagnetic order and b = 4 for the square lattice (see Section IV). || Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) optimizations employing M = 2^14 samples for the stochastic estimates were carried out using SR [58] with the linear algebra trick being in the regime P >> M [11, 20] enhanced with SPRING [107]. The optimization proceeded in three stages: 5000 steps without symmetry summation, followed by 500 steps including translational symmetries, and a final 100 steps with both rotational and reflection symmetries restored. The initial learning rate was set to eta = 5 x 10^-3 and gradually decreased during training. || The numerical experiments performed in this work required 25000 hours on GH200 GPUs. However, we point out that the preceding results obtained with other variational approaches, such as Gutzwiller Projected and RNN wave functions (see Table I), can be achieved with fewer than 1000 GPU hours. || This work was supported as part of the "Swiss AI initiative" by a grant from the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) under project ID a117 on Alps. RR and LLV acknowledge the CINECA award under the ISCRA initiative for the availability of high-performance computing resources and support. || arXiv:2602.02665 Sec. V.2: "n = L^2/b^2. In particular, we set b = 3 for the triangular lattice ... and b = 4 for the square lattice" ... "We take the attention weights to be translationally invariant across patches and enforce all remaining lattice symmetries, including translations within patches, rotations, and reflections (C6v group for the triangular lattice and C4v for the square lattice) through a projector operator in the trivial representation sector [106]." ... "Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) optimizations employing M = 2^14 samples for the stochastic estimates were carried out using SR [58] with the linear algebra trick being in the regime P ≫ M [11, 20] enhanced with SPRING [107]. The optimization proceeded in three stages: 5000 steps without symmetry summation, followed by 500 steps including translational symmetries, and a final 100 steps with both rotational and reflection symmetries restored."
